slides.title: An alert raises two different questions
slides.line: Does a 90% catch rate mean a 90% issue chance after an alert?
points: Distinguish the system's catch rate from the chance an alerted order has an issue.
Keep your prediction; we will use base rates to check it.
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands. Do not reveal the posterior yet; use the next slides to define outcomes and denominators.
slides.context: Synthetic order alerts: 1% of orders have an issue; the system flags 90% of those and 5% of ordinary orders.

slides.title: Predict which outcomes remain after an alert
slides.line: Which of the four order states include an alert?
points: List the complete cases first.
Do not assume the four cases are equally likely.
slides.notes: Give learners one minute to identify both alerted cases. Advance to the visual before discussing their shares.
slides.context: For one order, issue status and alert status form four possible combinations. Which two include an alert?

slides.title: A probability starts with a defined outcome
slides.context: One order has an issue or not, and receives an alert or not. These four states cover every order.

slides.title: An event is a set of outcomes
slides.context: For one fair die, the sample space S has six outcomes and the event E = even has three.
points: The sample space lists every possible result of one trial.
An event selects the results that answer the question.

slides.title: A model chance and an observed share differ
slides.context: Suppose a fair coin happens to land heads 48 times in 100 tosses.
points: The model describes the chance for a toss under its assumptions.
The observed share can differ in a finite sample without disproving fairness.

slides.title: Possible cases need not be equally likely
points: Count favorable outcomes only when the possible outcomes are equally likely.
Four named order states do not imply four equal probabilities.
slides.context: On a fair die, the even outcomes are 2, 4 and 6. Equal chances make counting a valid shortcut.

slides.title: Try the fair-die shortcut on a new event
points: The favorable outcomes are 4, 5 and 6.
This count works because every fair-die face has the same chance.
slides.context: For a fair die, “at least 4” means the outcomes 4, 5 and 6 out of six equally likely faces.

slides.title: Predict what OR does with overlap
slides.line: Should a shared outcome be counted once or twice?
points: Write the two event sets.
Circle outcomes that belong to both.
slides.notes: Have learners mark the overlap before showing the visual. Ask why simple addition can exceed the union.
slides.context: For a fair die, E means even and L means greater than 3. Outcomes 4 and 6 belong to both.

slides.title: AND keeps the overlap; OR counts it once
slides.context: On a fair die, E = {2, 4, 6} and L = {4, 5, 6}. The shared outcomes are 4 and 6.

slides.title: OR counts each shared outcome once
points: Adding the two groups counts 4 and 6 twice.
Subtract their two-outcome overlap once to get four distinct outcomes.
slides.context: For a fair die, E = {2, 4, 6} and L = {4, 5, 6}; the overlap is {4, 6}.

slides.title: Subtract the overlap in an OR question
slides.context: For a fair die, E = even and L = greater than 3; the overlap is {4, 6}.
slides.line: P(E ∪ L) = P(E) + P(L) − P(E ∩ L)
points: Adding the two event shares counts 4 and 6 twice.
The result is 3/6 + 3/6 − 2/6 = 4/6.

slides.title: Check inputs before calculating with them
slides.context: A proposed model assigns P(A) = 0.2, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.3.
points: An overlap cannot be larger than the smaller whole event.
Because 0.3 > 0.2, these three inputs cannot describe a valid model.

slides.title: A complement can shorten the calculation
points: The event and its complement partition the sample space.
Check that the two probabilities add to 1.
slides.context: For one fair die, the only way to roll a 6 has probability 1/6.

slides.title: Predict the number of complete meals
slides.line: Two bases, three proteins, three sauces: add or multiply?
points: Imagine choosing one option at each stage.
Count complete routes, not individual ingredients.
slides.notes: Ask learners to sketch one full route and predict the total before revealing the stage diagram.
slides.context: A meal has one base, one protein and one sauce. There are 2, 3 and 3 choices respectively.

slides.title: Multiply choices across stages
slides.context: A meal selects one base, one protein and one sauce.

slides.title: Multiply choices to count complete meals
points: Each meal uses one choice from each stage.
Every base–protein–sauce route is one distinct meal.
slides.context: There are 2 bases, 3 proteins and 3 sauces, with every combination allowed.

slides.title: The product rule needs a branch count at each stage
slides.context: If every earlier choice leaves the same number of options at the next stage, multiply those stage counts.
slides.line: N = n₁ × n₂ × n₃; here N = 2 × 3 × 3 = 18
points: Here n₁, n₂ and n₃ count the options at the three stages.
If a restriction changes later options, count the remaining branches for each earlier route.

slides.title: A restriction changes the branches you multiply
points: The two fillings are distinct, so only five remain for the second slot.
This counts ordered fillings; ignoring order answers another question.
slides.context: A sandwich has 3 breads and two ordered, distinct filling slots chosen from 6 fillings.

slides.title: Predict whether order changes the outcome
slides.line: Is assigning three roles the same as choosing a three-person team?
points: Imagine swapping two selected people.
Decide whether the result is a new outcome.
slides.notes: Have learners vote before advancing. A role assignment changes on a swap; a team does not.
slides.context: Five people are available. Compare assigning three distinct roles with choosing a three-person team.

slides.title: Order changes arrangements, not selections
slides.context: From five people, swapping selected people changes a role assignment but leaves a team unchanged.

slides.title: The question determines whether order matters
points: Roles make order matter. A team does not.
Divide by the reorderings of each selected team.
slides.context: Assign three distinct roles to five people; then count three-person teams without role labels.

slides.title: Use permutations when positions differ
slides.context: Five people can fill three distinct roles; no person fills more than one role.
points: The first, second and third roles have 5, 4 and 3 remaining choices.
Swapping two people changes the assignment.

slides.title: Divide out order when choosing a team
slides.context: The same five people can form an unordered three-person team.
points: Each team appears 3! = 6 times among ordered role assignments.
Thus 60 ordered assignments correspond to 60/6 = 10 teams.

slides.title: Two roles and two teammates have different counts
points: Swapping roles makes a new assignment.
Swapping names inside an unordered pair does not make a new team.
slides.context: From five people, compare two different roles with an unordered pair of teammates.

slides.title: Predict the denominator after given
slides.line: For on time given express, divide 15 by 80, 40 or 35?
points: Locate the express group first.
Keep the 15 express and on-time orders as the numerator.
slides.notes: Ask learners to choose a denominator without calculating. Reveal the order table on the next slide.
slides.context: In a separate synthetic table, 80 delivered orders include 40 express, 35 on time, and 15 both.

slides.title: Conditioning changes the denominator to the named group
slides.context: Among 80 delivered orders, 15 are both express and on time. “Given express” restricts us to 40.

slides.title: One count answers three different questions
points: 15/80 is both express and on time among all orders; 15/40 is on time given express.
15/35 is express given on time. Name the group before dividing.
slides.context: The 15 express-and-on-time orders belong to three groups: all 80 orders, 40 express orders and 35 on-time orders.

slides.title: Given B means divide within B
slides.context: In the 80-order table, A = on time, B = express, and 15 orders are both.
points: The vertical bar means “given B”: restrict the group to the 40 express orders.
The numerator keeps the 15 orders that are both express and on time.

slides.title: Reversing given changes the question
slides.context: The same table has 35 on-time orders, including 15 express orders.
points: “Express given on time” asks about the 35 on-time orders.
“On time given express” asks about the 40 express orders.

slides.title: Transfer the denominator rule to late express orders
points: The express group has 40 orders, 25 of them late.
The direction of conditioning determines which group is counted.
slides.context: Of the 40 express orders, 25 were late and 15 were on time.

slides.title: Independence means new information does not change the chance
slides.context: In the 80-order table, ask whether knowing the service changes the chance of on-time delivery.

slides.title: Check independence with conditional and joint shares
slides.line: P(A | B) = P(A) when B gives no new information
points: The joint check is P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
Disjoint nonempty events cannot be independent.
slides.context: Independence means the on-time chance within express matches the on-time chance overall; check with the table.

slides.title: The table does not support independence
slides.context: In the 80-order table, 15 of 40 express orders and 35 of all 80 orders are on time.
points: Knowing the service changes the observed on-time share.
This comparison alone does not establish that service caused the difference.

slides.title: A joint share provides the same check
slides.context: In the 80-order table, P(express) = 40/80 and P(on time) = 35/80.
points: If the events were independent, the joint share would equal the product.
Here 0.1875 differs from 0.21875; the sample events are not independent.

slides.title: Predict which paths produce an alert
slides.line: Can an alert come from both an issue and an ordinary order?
points: Name the two disjoint routes.
Multiply along each route before adding.
slides.notes: Ask learners to identify both alert routes. Do not show the total until the weighted-path slide.
slides.context: Return to a separate alert model: 1% issues, a 90% issue catch rate and a 5% ordinary-order flag rate.

slides.title: Weight each path before adding its contribution
slides.context: An alert can follow either an issue order or an ordinary order; each path has its own weight.

slides.title: Total probability adds the weighted paths
points: Multiply within each issue-status path.
Add the two disjoint alert paths: 585 alerts per 10,000 expected orders.
slides.context: In the alert model, 1% of orders have issues; 90% of those alert. Of the remaining 99%, 5% alert.

slides.title: Total probability sums disjoint paths
slides.context: I = issue and A = alert in the separate synthetic alert model.
slides.line: P(A) = P(I)P(A | I) + P(not I)P(A | not I)
points: The two paths to an alert cannot occur together and cover all alerts.
Weight each conditional rate by the share entering its path.

slides.title: Expected counts make the base rate visible
slides.context: In 10,000 expected orders, the model gives 100 issues and 9,900 ordinary orders.
points: The catch rate applies to 100 issue orders, not to all alerts.
The ordinary group is much larger, so it contributes more alerts.

slides.title: Use the complement to count no-alert orders
points: Alert and no alert cover every order in this model.
That is 9,415 no-alert orders per 10,000 expected orders.
slides.context: The alert model gives P(alert) = 0.0585, so every other order is in the no-alert group.

slides.title: Predict the issue share among alerts
slides.line: Are most alerted orders real issues?
points: Compare the 90 issue alerts with the 495 ordinary-order alerts.
What fraction of all 585 alerts came from issues?
slides.notes: Ask learners for a prediction before showing the Bayes tree. Do not reveal the calculated posterior in Notes.
slides.context: Among 10,000 expected orders, 90 issue orders and 495 ordinary orders raise an alert.

slides.title: Bayes reverses the question using base rates
slides.context: The tree shows 90 issue alerts and 495 ordinary alerts per 10,000 expected orders.

slides.title: An alert changes the chance, not the decision
points: The alert catches 90% of real issues; that is a different conditional chance.
Among alerted orders, most are ordinary because ordinary orders are far more common.
slides.context: Among 585 alerted orders, only 90 have issues. The 90% catch rate uses a different denominator.

slides.title: Bayes divides the issue path by all alerts
slides.context: The issue-alert path has chance 0.01 × 0.90; the ordinary-alert path has 0.99 × 0.05.
points: The numerator is the chance of an issue and an alert together.
The denominator includes every route that produces an alert.

slides.title: Calculate the posterior from both paths
slides.context: Let I mean issue and A mean alert. Keep the 1% issue base rate, 90% catch rate and 5% ordinary-order alert rate.
points: The issue-alert path contributes 0.009 of all orders.
Among alerts, about 15.4% indicate an issue under this model.

slides.title: A different base rate changes the answer
slides.context: Let I mean issue and A mean alert. Hypothetically raise the issue base rate to 5%; keep both alert rates fixed.
points: The system performs the same within each issue-status group.
The alerted group now contains a larger issue share because issues are less rare.

slides.title: Reverse the question for a negative alert
points: The denominator includes every no-alert order.
A negative alert lowers the issue chance without making it zero.
slides.context: Among 10,000 expected orders, 10 issue orders and 9,405 ordinary orders receive no alert.

slides.title: Odds compare an event with its alternative
slides.context: A separate example starts with a 40% issue chance and a positive signal twice as likely with an issue.

slides.title: Convert probability to odds before updating
points: Turn probability into odds before applying the evidence multiplier.
Convert the updated odds back to probability.
slides.context: In the 40% prior example, a positive signal has likelihood ratio 0.8/0.4 = 2.

slides.title: Odds compare an event with its opposite
slides.context: In a separate signal example, the prior chance of an issue is 40%.
points: Probability compares issues with all cases.
Odds compare issues directly with nonissues.

slides.title: A likelihood ratio scales prior odds
slides.context: A positive signal occurs with probability 0.8 for issues and 0.4 for nonissues.
points: The ratio says how much more likely the signal is under an issue.
Convert 4:3 odds back to probability: 4/(4 + 3) ≈ 57.1%.

slides.title: Predict what a second signal requires
slides.line: Can the same evidence multiplier be used twice automatically?
points: Ask whether signals are independent within each issue-status group.
Dependence changes the second signal's likelihood ratio.
slides.notes: Invite an explanation of what could make two signals related. The next slide makes the assumption explicit.
slides.context: After one positive signal, ask whether a second positive signal provides the same new evidence.

slides.title: A second signal updates odds
slides.context: Multiply by a second likelihood ratio only if signals are independent within each issue-status group.

slides.title: A second signal needs a dependence assumption
points: A second signal multiplies odds only under the stated conditional-independence assumption.
Without that assumption, use the second signal’s conditional rates after the first.
slides.context: Starting from 4:3 odds after one positive signal, a second conditionally independent positive doubles the odds.

slides.title: Two updates need a conditional assumption
slides.context: Let S₁ and S₂ be positive signals, and I be an issue.
slides.line: P(S₂ | I, S₁) = P(S₂ | I) only under conditional independence
points: The matching equality must also hold in the nonissue group.
Without both equalities, the second likelihood ratio need not equal the first.

slides.title: Use new conditional rates when signals depend
slides.context: Suppose the second signal is related to the first; its rates after S₁ must be measured.
slides.line: LR₂ = P(S₂ | I, S₁) / P(S₂ | not I, S₁)
points: Multiply the current odds by this conditional ratio.
Reusing the first ratio without evidence can overstate the update.

slides.title: A negative second signal can reverse the update
points: The negative likelihood ratio is 1/3 under the same conditional-independence assumption.
Evidence can move a probability down as well as up.
slides.context: Starting from 4:3 odds, a negative second signal has rates 0.2 with an issue and 0.6 without.

slides.title: An alert decision needs probability and consequences
slides.context: Return to the original alert model: 90 of 585 alerts indicate a real issue.

slides.title: Report the posterior, assumptions and missing costs
slides.line: 15.4% issue chance among alerts ≠ a business decision
points: Report the model, base rate and uncertainty.
Compare review cost, missed-issue cost and available capacity before acting.
slides.context: An alerted order has a 15.4% modeled issue chance; the action also depends on consequences.

slides.title: A decision compares expected consequences
slides.context: Let p be the issue chance for an alerted order. Hypothetically, review costs $5, catches every issue and missing one costs $50.
slides.line: Expected missed-issue cost = p × $50; review cost = $5
points: This simplified example omits other costs and capacity limits.
Review is favored when the expected avoided loss exceeds the review cost.

slides.title: Derive the review threshold from the costs
slides.context: Let p be the issue chance for an alert. Use only the hypothetical $5 review cost and $50 missed-issue loss.
points: The original alert posterior of 15.4% exceeds this illustrative threshold.
Change the costs or review effectiveness and the threshold changes.

slides.title: A model probability needs a reality check
slides.context: The 15.4% is conditional on the original 1% base rate and alert performance.
points: Check whether the current order population still matches the model.
Report sensitivity to the base rate and to the consequences of an error.

slides.title: Close with the question before the percentage
points: State which population and event the probability describes.
Then explain what additional costs or consequences the business decision needs.
slides.context: Before a business action, name the event and group, calculate the chance, then compare consequences.

slides.title: Predict the independent sample size
slides.line: Twelve orders, each timed twice: 12 or 24 independent units?
points: Name the unit that received a process assignment.
Repeated readings of one unit can be related.
slides.notes: Ask learners to vote before revealing the order plot. Count assigned orders, not stopwatch readings.
slides.context: A packing company assigns 12 orders to three processes, then records each order twice.

slides.title: Keep each order with its process
slides.context: Synthetic packing times: Process A has four orders, B has four, and C has four; each dot is an order.

slides.title: The observation unit determines what can be compared
points: Keep each time attached to its process.
Repeated readings of one order do not create new independent orders.
slides.context: The packing comparison uses 12 independent assigned orders across three processes, not repeated stopwatch readings.

slides.title: The global null concerns population means
slides.context: The packing case compares processing time for independent orders assigned to A, B or C.
slides.line: H₀: μA = μB = μC; H₁: at least one differs
points: Sample means of 20, 24 and 27 minutes do not prove population means differ.
ANOVA compares their separation with the noise among orders within processes.

slides.title: The baseline depends on the question
slides.context: Packing-process means are 20, 24 and 27 minutes; each process has four orders.

slides.title: The grand mean weights all observed orders
points: ANOVA weights each observed order.
An equal-weight average of group means answers a different question when group sizes differ.
slides.context: Across the 12 packing orders, process totals are 80, 96 and 108 minutes.

slides.title: Weight group means by their order counts
slides.context: For groups with counts nᵢ and means x̄ᵢ, the grand mean gives every observed order equal weight.
points: Here N = 12 orders; equal group sizes also allow (20 + 24 + 27)/3.
With unequal group sizes, use the order counts rather than averaging group means equally.

slides.title: Predict where noise enters the comparison
slides.line: Could the same group means give weaker evidence?
points: Hold the group means fixed.
Imagine a wider spread of orders within each process.
slides.notes: Ask for a prediction before drawing the variation split. The noisy alternative appears later.
slides.context: Imagine two packing datasets with the same group means but different spread inside each process.

slides.title: Each order has a group gap and a within-group gap
slides.context: Each packing time differs from its process mean; each process mean differs from the overall mean.

slides.title: The squared gaps split total variation
points: Total squared variation splits into between-group and within-group sums.
The within-group part is the noise estimate for the comparison.
slides.context: For the 12 packing orders, total squared variation is 122⅔ minutes².

slides.title: Between-group variation measures mean gaps
slides.context: Each packing process has four orders; the group means are 20, 24 and 27, and the grand mean is 23⅔.
slides.line: SSbetween = Σ nᵢ( x̄ᵢ − x̄ )² = 98⅔ minutes²
points: Here nᵢ is a group count, x̄ᵢ its mean and x̄ the grand mean.
Larger gaps between group means increase this signal component.

slides.title: Within-group variation measures residual gaps
slides.context: For each packing order, compare its time with the mean of its own process.
points: Here xᵢⱼ is an order time and x̄ᵢ is its process mean.
It estimates noise for the global comparison when model assumptions hold.

slides.title: Mean squares divide variation by degrees of freedom
points: Three group means leave 2 between-group degrees of freedom.
Twelve orders minus three fitted group means leave 9 within-group degrees of freedom.
slides.context: The packing comparison has three groups and 12 independent orders; divide each variation sum by its degrees of freedom.

slides.title: Degrees of freedom count free comparisons
slides.context: The packing case has k = 3 process means and N = 12 independent orders.
points: The three mean deviations from the grand mean obey one constraint.
Fitting three group means leaves nine independent residual directions.

slides.title: The same group gap can have different noise
slides.context: The chart holds packing-process means fixed while increasing the spread of orders inside groups.

slides.title: F compares between-group signal with within-group noise
points: The ratio compares mean separation with within-group noise.
More noise can make the same mean gaps less persuasive.
slides.context: For packing times, between-group mean square is 49⅓ and within-group mean square is 2⅔ minutes².

slides.title: F is a ratio of two mean squares
slides.context: For packing times, MSbetween = 49⅓ and MSwithin = 2⅔ minutes².
points: The squared-minute units cancel, leaving a unitless statistic.
Under equal population means and the model, a large ratio is unusual.

slides.title: The F reference needs a defensible design
slides.context: The 12 packing orders must provide independent units for the ordinary one-way F test.
slides.line: Independent errors + comparable variances + suitable residual shape
points: Random assignment or sampling supports the population interpretation.
Inspect residuals and spread; a small synthetic example does not verify assumptions.

slides.title: Four times the within-group noise cuts F fourfold
points: The group means stay fixed while within-group SS rises from 24 to 96.
The evidence weakens even though the observed mean gaps do not move.
slides.context: Hold the observed process means fixed, but raise within-group squared variation from 24 to 96 minutes².

slides.title: The reference curve puts F in context
slides.context: Under equal population process means, compare the observed F = 18.5 with an F distribution having 2 and 9 degrees of freedom.

slides.title: A right-tail area measures evidence under the null
points: Use the right tail of the F reference under equal population means.
The 5% cutoff is 4.2565; it is not the observed p-value.
slides.context: The packing null says all three population means are equal. The observed F statistic is 18.5.

slides.title: A p-value is conditional on the null
slides.context: In the packing case, F = 18.5 with 2 and 9 degrees of freedom.
points: This is the chance of a statistic at least this extreme if the null model holds.
It is not the probability that the null is true.

slides.title: An observed variance share is descriptive
slides.context: For packing orders, SSbetween = 98⅔ and SStotal = 122⅔ minutes².
points: This describes the share of variation attributed to process in these twelve observations.
It does not by itself prove causation or predict the share in new orders.

slides.title: The noisy alternative sits near the 5% threshold
points: The right-tail area is much larger than for F = 18.5.
A 5% rejection still says nothing by itself about useful minutes saved.
slides.context: With the same process means but four times the noise, the hypothetical F statistic is 4.625.

slides.title: A global signal does not name the winning group
slides.context: For packing times, the global F test asks whether all three process population means could be equal.

slides.title: State the global conclusion within its scope
points: There is evidence that the population means are not all equal.
The global test does not identify every pairwise difference or a causal winner.
slides.context: The packing analysis finds a global mean difference across A, B and C; it has not named every differing pair.

slides.title: A planned pair needs an adjusted interval
points: The 4-minute sample gap gets a Bonferroni-adjusted margin of 3.387 minutes.
Plan all three pairs as one family; under the model, their intervals have at least 95% simultaneous coverage.
slides.context: In the packing case, B averages 24 minutes and A averages 20; A–B, A–C and B–C form one planned family.

slides.title: Plan the comparison family before looking
slides.context: For the three packing processes, the family A–B, A–C and B–C has m = 3 comparisons.
points: Bonferroni controls the family chance of at least one false rejection at 5%.
A planned contrast can be tested directly; an omnibus F result is not a mandatory gate.

slides.title: A pairwise estimate needs an uncertainty band
slides.context: In the packing case, B averages 24 minutes and A averages 20; both have four orders.
points: MSE is within-group mean square: 2⅔ minutes²; the estimated difference is four minutes.
The adjusted interval shown earlier is 4 ± 3.387 minutes.

slides.title: Predict how many cells the design needs
slides.line: Two offers × two day types: how many combinations?
points: Draw every offer–day pairing.
Ask what replication each pairing needs.
slides.notes: Have learners sketch the four cells before showing the grid. Keep the separate retailer dataset distinct from the packing case.
slides.context: A separate retailer example crosses two offers with two day types; draw all offer-by-day combinations.

slides.title: A two-factor design observes every combination
slides.context: The retailer case has Standard and Bundle offers on weekdays and weekends: four cells in total.

slides.title: Replication belongs within each factor combination
points: All four combinations must be observed.
Independent replication within each cell supplies the error estimate.
slides.context: The retailer case records three independent transactions in each of four offer-by-day cells.

slides.title: Cell means can differ from marginal means
slides.context: Retailer spending differs by both offer and day: four cell means are $20, $26, $24 and $38.

slides.title: Compare offers within each day type first
points: Each subtraction compares Bundle with Standard on the same day type.
The equal-day average gain of $8 does not describe either day by itself.
slides.context: Retailer sample mean spending: Standard/Bundle is $20/$24 on weekdays and $26/$38 on weekends.

slides.title: Marginal means average across another factor
slides.context: Retailer cell means are Standard weekday $20, Standard weekend $26, Bundle weekday $24, Bundle weekend $38.
points: Equal cell replication gives each day equal weight in these sample margins.
The $8 average offer difference can hide different weekday and weekend gains.

slides.title: A future day mix changes the average gain
points: The equal-day $8 gain assumes a 50–50 day mix.
This is a spending estimate for a hypothetical mix, not profit or a new observation.
slides.context: The hypothetical future sales mix is 75% weekdays and 25% weekends; observed cell means stay the same.

slides.title: Main effects may miss a combination effect
slides.context: The retailer example has an overall mean of $27, but the offer effect may depend on the day.

slides.title: Interaction corrects an additive cell prediction
points: The grand mean and main-effect adjustments predict $36 for Bundle weekends.
The +$2 is this cell's adjustment; the full change in Bundle gain across days is $8.
slides.context: The observed Bundle-weekend sample mean is $38. An additive model using the grand, offer and day effects predicts $36.

slides.title: Interaction is the leftover after main effects
slides.context: In the retailer case, grand mean is $27; Bundle main adjustment is +$4 and weekend adjustment is +$5.
points: The observed Bundle-weekend cell mean is $38.
The +$2 interaction adjustment closes the gap for that cell.

slides.title: Predict whether interaction lines must cross
slides.line: If the offer gain changes by day, must the lines cross?
points: Compare their slopes rather than their endpoints alone.
Predict what nonparallel lines would mean.
slides.notes: Ask for a sketch of two nonparallel lines that do not cross in the plotted range. Reveal the chart next.
slides.context: In the retailer example, Bundle adds $4 on weekdays but $12 on weekends. Predict the line pattern.

slides.title: Interaction changes an effect across contexts
slides.context: The retailer offer gain changes from $4 on weekdays to $12 on weekends; compare the two slopes.

slides.title: A marginal average can hide a useful interaction
points: Nonparallel lines show changing sample effects; they need not cross.
A marginal average can conceal a valuable context-specific effect.
slides.context: Across retailer days, the average Bundle gain is $8, although neither day has an $8 gain.

slides.title: Subtract the two gains to measure interaction
slides.context: In the retailer sample, Bundle raises spending by $4 on weekdays and $12 on weekends.
points: The $8 contrast is how much the Bundle gain changes across day types.
It happens to equal the $8 equal-day average gain; the two numbers answer different questions.

slides.title: Keep interaction separate from random error
slides.context: For 12 independent retailer transactions, split squared variation (SS) into offer, day, interaction and within-cell error.

slides.title: Four variation sources add to the total
points: Separate offer, day, interaction and within-cell error variation.
With 8 residual degrees of freedom, MSE = 32/8 = 4 dollars².
slides.context: In the balanced retailer design, squared variation totals 572 dollars² across all 12 transactions.

slides.title: The balanced two-way design partitions freedom
slides.context: The retailer has two offer levels, two day levels and three independent transactions in each of four cells.
slides.line: df: offer 1; day 1; interaction 1; error 8; total 11
points: Four fitted cell means leave 12 − 4 = 8 residual degrees of freedom.
The source degrees of freedom add to the total: 1 + 1 + 1 + 8 = 11.

slides.title: Divide each source by its own freedom
slides.context: Retailer sums of squares are 192 offer, 300 day, 48 interaction and 32 error dollars².
points: Each effect has one degree of freedom in this 2 × 2 design.
The same within-cell error mean square is the denominator for all three F tests.

slides.title: An interaction contrast measures the changing gain
points: The difference of differences isolates the changing bundle gain.
Its standard error is about $2.31; the matching interaction F is 12.
slides.context: The retailer interaction compares the $12 weekend Bundle gain with the $4 weekday gain.

slides.title: Noise puts the $8 interaction in context
slides.context: The retailer design has three independent transactions per cell and MSE = 4 dollars².
points: The contrast adds four cell means, each estimated from three transactions.
The standardized contrast is about 8/2.31 = 3.46.

slides.title: The contrast and ANOVA interaction agree
slides.context: For the retailer data, the interaction contrast is $8 with standard error √(16/3) ≈ $2.31.
points: With one interaction degree of freedom, the squared t statistic equals the ANOVA F statistic.
The right-tail F p-value is about 0.0085 under the model.

slides.title: One ANOVA table answers three different questions
slides.context: The retailer ANOVA table tests offer, day and their interaction against the same within-cell noise.

slides.title: Name each null before reading its F test
slides.line: F offer = 48  ·  F day = 75  ·  F interaction = 12
points: Each row tests a different null hypothesis.
Interpret interaction before promising one universal offer effect.
slides.context: For retailer spending, offer, day and interaction are three separate null questions.

slides.title: Read each ANOVA row as a distinct claim
slides.context: The retailer table contains rows for offer, day and offer-by-day interaction.
slides.line: H₀ offer: average offer effect = 0; H₀ day: average day effect = 0; H₀ interaction: effect does not change
points: Each F statistic answers its own null question.
Interpret interaction before reporting one universal offer effect.

slides.title: Repeated readings need not be independent replications
slides.context: In the retailer design, each cell needs independent transactions; repeated readings are not new sales.

slides.title: Count independent units before trusting the table
slides.line: 12 independent transactions − 4 cell means = 8 error df
points: Counting duplicate records as independent inflates information.
Check assignment, residuals and similar error spread before trusting the table.
slides.context: The retailer has 12 independent transactions and fits four cell means, leaving eight error degrees of freedom.

slides.title: Check the residuals, not only the F values
slides.context: The retailer ANOVA assumes independent transactions and a suitable common error model across four cells.
slides.line: Residual = observed spending − fitted cell mean
points: Compare residual spread across cells and look for strong outliers or patterns.
Repeated customers or shifts may require a different dependence model.

slides.title: One observation per cell leaves no error estimate
slides.line: 4 observations − 4 fitted cell means = 0 error df
points: A complete 2 × 2 grid alone is not independent replication.
Without residual degrees of freedom, this simple design cannot estimate within-cell error.
slides.context: A hypothetical retailer dataset with one transaction in each of four cells has no within-cell replication.

slides.title: A recommendation can depend on the combination
slides.context: The retailer Bundle raises sample spending by $4 on weekdays and $12 on weekends, before costs.

slides.title: Name what the spending data cannot decide
points: Estimate uncertainty around each gain before projecting it to future transactions.
A policy also needs contribution margins, Bundle cost and the expected mix of day types.
slides.context: The retailer sample measures spending per transaction. The business goal is a profitable offer policy.

slides.title: Spending lift is not profit lift
slides.context: Retailer sample spending increases by $4 on weekdays and $12 on weekends with Bundle.
slides.line: Net value needs margin, offer cost and future day mix
points: The observed dollar figures are spending per transaction, not contribution margin.
A statistically detectable interaction alone cannot choose the offer policy.

slides.title: Match the recommendation to the future mix
slides.context: Hypothetically, 75% of future transactions occur on weekdays and 25% on weekends.
points: The $6 is a mix-weighted spending estimate from the sample effects.
Compare it with costs and uncertainty before making a business decision.

slides.title: Audit software output against the study design
slides.line: Check the model pieces before the software tail area
points: One-way: SSG = 98⅔, SSW = 24, F = 18.5.
Two-way: error df = 8, MSE = 4, interaction F = 12.
slides.context: Before trusting software output, match its rows, units and error degrees of freedom to the study design.
